"Par" means a standard, expected level — a fixed reference point that things are measured against. Think of it as a benchmark: a line in the middle that represents "normal" or "equal." Everything else is either above it, exactly at it, or below it.

This single idea runs through every use of the word, no matter the context.

In everyday English, "par" almost always appears inside a few common phrases, so let's go through each one.

"On par with" (or "on a par with") means equal to, or at the same level as, something else. If you say her cooking is on par with a restaurant chef's, you mean her cooking is just as good.

"Up to par" means meeting the expected or acceptable standard. Work that is "up to par" is as good as it should be. Work that is "not up to par" falls short.

"Below par" in everyday speech means worse than the normal or expected standard. You'll often hear it used to describe not feeling well — someone says "I'm feeling a bit below par today," meaning they feel worse than usual.

"Par for the course" is a very common phrase meaning exactly what you'd expect in a given situation — something typical, neither surprising nor special. If your bus is late again and you say "that's par for the course," you mean it's completely normal and unsurprising.

This is where the word is most precisely defined, and where it originally comes from in the sense we use today.

In golf, par is the number of strokes (individual shots) that a highly skilled, expert-level golfer is expected to need to complete a hole — or an entire course — under normal conditions. It is the benchmark for expert play. Every hole on a golf course is assigned its own par number, which reflects how long and difficult that hole is.

A par-3 hole is short. An expert is expected to reach the green in one shot and then sink the ball in two putts, for a total of 3 strokes.

A par-4 hole is medium length. The expectation is two shots to reach the green, then two putts — 4 strokes total.

A par-5 hole is long. The expectation is three shots to reach the green, then two putts — 5 strokes total.

Notice that every hole builds in two putts as a standard assumption. That's a consistent rule built into how par is calculated.

A full 18-hole golf course has a total par, which is the sum of the pars of all 18 holes — typically 70, 71, or 72 for most standard courses.

Now, golfers' scores are always discussed relative to par. If a hole is par 4 and you finish it in exactly 4 strokes, you scored par — right on the benchmark. If you finish it in 3 strokes (one fewer than expected), you scored a birdie, and you are "one under par." Two under par on a single hole is called an eagle. On the other side, one stroke more than par is called a bogey, and two strokes more is a double bogey.

Over a full round, golfers track their total strokes relative to the course's total par. A final score of "six under par" (written as −6) means the golfer needed six fewer strokes than par — a strong performance. "Four over par" means they needed four extra strokes — a weaker performance.

Here is an important distinction to keep in mind: in golf, being "under par" is a good thing, because you used fewer strokes than expected. But in everyday language, "below par" means something bad. Same idea, opposite emotional meaning depending on context — so always notice which world you're in.

In finance, "par" — also written as "par value" or "face value" — refers to the stated, official value of a financial security as declared by whoever issued it. It is the reference number printed on the document, representing what the security is nominally worth at the time of issue.

For bonds: a bond is essentially a loan. A company or government borrows money from investors and promises to pay it back at a specific future date (called the maturity date). The amount they promise to repay is the par value of the bond. Most bonds have a par value of $1,000. If you buy a bond "at par," you pay $1,000, you receive interest payments along the way, and at maturity, you get your $1,000 back.

But bonds trade in markets, and their price shifts constantly based on interest rates and other factors. When a bond's market price is higher than its par value — say, it costs $1,080 — it is said to be trading "above par" or at a premium. This usually happens when the bond offers a more attractive interest rate than what's currently available elsewhere, so investors are willing to pay more for it. When a bond's price is lower than its par value — say, $920 — it is trading "below par" or at a discount, usually because its interest rate is less attractive than current alternatives.

For stocks: companies also assign a par value to their shares, but for stocks, this is largely a legal and accounting technicality. Stock par values are often set at a very small number — like $0.01 per share — and have almost no relationship to the stock's actual price in the market. You don't need to think about stock par value in most practical conversations about investing.

The phrase you'll encounter most often in finance is simply "at par," meaning at face value — no discount, no premium.

Every use of "par" traces back to the same root idea: a standard, expected, or equal level used as a reference point. In everyday language it shows up in phrases about meeting expectations or being equal to something. In golf it is the expert-level stroke count for a hole or course, and your score is always described relative to it. In finance it is the official face value of a security, and prices are compared against it. Once you see that central idea — a benchmark, a point of equality, a standard — the word clicks into place in any context you encounter it.
